<reason>A won a close, high-quality clash by tying the motion to lived pressure—the package, the aunt, the “actual wedding”—and showing B’s purified rite is not what obligation actually enforces. B’s form-versus-invoice frame was the debate’s clearest idea and stayed live, but A’s inseparability argument forced B into a costly kin-facing duty that walked back “tradition never asks for debt,” while sting-as-enforcement could not be cleanly capped. A’s elopement answer overextended, yet “little obligation” still tracked the motion better than B’s claim that any release from public form collapses the whole duty.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s first rebuttal that the inherited tradition cannot be quarantined from its enforcement (guest lists, “when’s the actual wedding?”), which turned B’s modest examples into exceptions to the rule they called binding.</best_rebuttal>
